transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Flores (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (AtlasRetail Platform), Evan Zhao (Atlas SRE), Leila Martin (Atlas Product)

Summary (auto): weekly POC check-in; focus on repeated short burst 5xx/timeouts; discussed probe warmup, concurrency, and fallback routing.

00:00:00 Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to focus today on the short bursts you saw last week where a bunch of requests hit and you saw elevated 502s and timeouts, so Diego and I will run through what we observed and some mitigations.
00:00:28 Maya (Customer): Yeah thanks, main symptom is when traffic jumps — like marketing pushes or batch calls — we get a flurry of 504s, also some 502s, and then latency slowly recovers. It's hurting storefront features.
00:00:48 Diego (SE): Ok, quick restate: we looked at telemetry from last Tuesday — there were repeated small spikes of concurrent requests hitting a cold shard, KV cache miss rates spiked and we saw queue depth grow, then we hit a hard limit at the per-model concurrency and the runtime returned 502s under load.
00:01:10 Evan (SRE): I want to underline that we see this reproducibly when our canary job hits the service; but there are also these probe patterns — our health checks are very aggressive, they try to warm endpoints and maybe amplify the spike.
00:01:28 Jordan: Right, probes can be a double-edged sword. If they're uncoordinated they can cause warm-up traffic that collides with real requests. Diego, walk through the three mitigations we recommended.
00:01:40 Diego: Sure. Short version: 1) Probe warmup: move from constant aggressive probes to a graduated warmup script that ramps containers/models before traffic. 2) Per-route concurrency caps and soft-queueing: reduce hard failures by increasing queue window and allowing short buffering. 3) Conditional fallback routing: if a model variant is near saturation, route to a smaller quantized variant with slightly higher latency but no errors.
00:02:12 Leila (Product): For the fallback, can we pick which features degrade? e.g., route non-critical autocomplete to cheaper variant but keep checkout on the primary?
00:02:25 Diego: Yes, routing policies support per-route and per-feature tagging, you can define conditions (e.g., queue depth > 80% or p95 latency > 1.5s) and a policy to route to fallback. Implementation detail: need to ensure KV cache compatibility or accept cold cache on fallback.
00:02:48 Evan: That cache thing worries me — if fallback misses the cache we might actually see worse tail latency on certain flows.
00:03:00 Diego: Good call. One of the things we suggested is a pre-warm for the fallback model in the background once the condition triggers, plus a short-lived prefix cache transfer where supported. For some models we also recommend keeping a tiny steady-state warm pool so cold starts are bounded.
00:03:22 Maya: Can you clarify "prefix cache transfer"? I think our infra team — we might have called it K-V cash in previous notes — the transcript had a weird spelling, lol.
00:03:36 Diego: Yeah it's KV cache, stands for key-value cache of past tokens. Transfer means using shared storage of commonly used prefixes or pre-populating the model cache on the fallback nodes. It's not instant but can be fast if we copy top N prefixes for your top routes.
00:03:56 Jordan: Quick pause — are we all aligned that root cause blend is: probe pattern + cold shards + concurrency hard limits, and fallback routing mis-configuration made it worse?
00:04:08 Evan: Agreed. Also our client-side retry strategy was too aggressive; it retried immediately which doubled the incoming burst.
00:04:18 Leila: So we have four levers: 1) adjust probes, 2) change retry-backoff on client, 3) per-route concurrency / queueing, 4) fallback routing and prewarm. Correct?
00:04:29 Diego: Yup. We recommended a safe sequence: probes -> client retry backoff -> concurrency caps -> fallback rules, because each step reduces the chance of further pressure while we test the next.
00:04:44 Maya: Can you share the probe script? We currently have a k8s readiness prob that pings every 10s with a token; maybe that's too often.
00:04:53 Diego: We'll send a small warmup script that does an exponential ramp over 60s and then a periodic low-rate keepalive. I'll paste examples in the notes.
00:05:04 Jordan: For today's call, Diego prepared a quick demo of a synthetic probe run and a concurrency cap simulation.
00:05:12 Diego: Right — I'm going to describe results: baseline without warmup — synthetic burst of 2k RPS — p95 jumps to 1.8s and 502s hit ~1.6% during first 90s. With graduated warmup enabled we saw p95 peak at 0.9s and 502s drop to 0.05%. So warmup gives big wins.
00:05:39 Evan: Those differences are promising, can we reproduce in our environment? Our traffic shape has very spiky tails and small long-running sessions hitting different prefixes.
00:05:50 Diego: You can reproduce, but need to match the prefix distribution — if you have long-tail corpus we'll want to pre-seed the warm pool with your top 500 prefixes.
00:06:05 Leila: How intrusive is that pre-seeding? Any data privacy concerns?
00:06:12 Diego: Pre-seeding uses hashed prefixes and only stores token-level stats, not the whole input payload. If you prefer we can do it from your side privately — you run the seeding script and upload only cold-start metrics.
00:06:26 Maya: Ok. On retries — we discovered our front-end retries every 200ms up to 3 times. Should change to exponential backoff?
00:06:35 Jordan: Yes 200ms is too aggressive. Try 250-500ms base with jitter and cap; Diego recommended 800ms cap for your flows. That prevents causing a retry storm.
00:06:48 Evan: Also request priority: can Redwood runtime respect a priority flag so we can mark checkout flows as high-priority?
00:06:56 Diego: Yes, we support priority headers which map to a prioritized processing queue. That can be part of the per-route policy. We'll document header names.
00:07:10 Maya: About per-route concurrency caps: do we need to know the exact concurrency limits per model? We saw a config file that had global 64 concurrency per model.
00:07:20 Diego: Global 64 is a good starting point; we suggest per-route caps lower than global to protect critical routes — e.g., checkout route cap 8, search autocomplete cap 12. These numbers depend on your traffic and model size.
00:07:37 Leila: Where do autoscaling and dedicated pool factors come in? If we had reserved capacity would this still happen?
00:07:45 Jordan: Reserved capacity reduces the chance of evicting warm shards, but very short burst/cold-shard behavior can still surface if the request lands on an idle instance. Dedicated reduces risk but doesn't remove need for warmup and good retry policies.
00:07:59 Evan: Ok makes sense. Any quick wins to reduce 502s this week?
00:08:04 Diego: Yes: immediate wins — disable aggressive readiness probes, add client-side jittered retry backoff, and add a tiny warm pool (1–2 warm instances per critical model) while we test. We can push the warm-pool change in a config toggle for Dedicated or Hosted.
00:08:20 Maya: Can Redwood enable the warm pool toggle on our pilot environment?
00:08:25 Jordan: Yes, we can enable it for the pilot account. Diego will need your access/namespace to do it or we can send instructions for you to enable.
00:08:35 Evan: We'll share access. Also we want to see better telemetry: queue depth, per-route concurrency runtime, and per-node cache hit rates. Currently our ingestion only included latency and errors.
00:08:47 Diego: We'll add those metrics to the pilot dashboard: queue_depth, concurrency_inflight, kv_cache_hit_rate, and fallback_trigger_count. Expect a patch to the console in 48 hours.
00:09:02 Leila: Can you put an alert recipe for when fallback triggers more than 3x in 10m?
00:09:08 Diego: Yep, we'll create an alert rule.
00:09:12 Jordan: Quick note on telemetry retention — if you need long retention for audits, we can export raw traces to your S3 with role-based access. That is an enterprise add-on.
00:09:25 Maya: Not for this pilot, but good to know.
00:09:30 Diego: I want to surface one subtlety: warmup reduces cold-start errors, but if the request distribution changes (new product, new phrase) the prefix coverage matters. So it's not a silver bullet. We'll pair warmup with a light-weight sampling pilot to monitor unseen prefixes.
00:09:49 Evan: Sampling pilot — do you mean keep a tiny traffic stream that runs through a warmed path?
00:09:55 Diego: Exactly, a small percentage of traffic is routed through a prewarmed path used to keep caches hot for top prefixes.
00:10:04 Leila: Let's talk about fallback quality regressions — if fallback model is quantized it may hallucinate more or lose fidelity. How do we guard against that?
00:10:14 Diego: We recommend a fallback policy that prefers pragmatic degradation: for low-risk endpoints (autocomplete, suggestions) use smaller variant; for high-risk (checkout, legal copy generation) fail-open to a small-rate limited queue or block and fail with a user-friendly message. Also set up evals to compare output quality periodically and alert on regressions.
00:10:36 Jordan: Any legal or compliance concerns about routing to different models?
00:10:40 Maya: From data residency perspective we need to ensure primary and fallback are in same region, else data residency policies break.
00:10:48 Diego: Good call — routing policies can be constrained by region tags, so we won't move cross-region unless you approve. We'll include that in the config suggestions.
00:11:00 Evan: Let's pin a concrete experiment plan. Proposal: 1) Toggle warm pool on pilot 2) Deploy probe warmup script 3) Adjust client retry backoff and add jitter 4) Run 10k synthetic probes to capture cold-start metrics 5) Evaluate fallback policy on a small route.
00:11:20 Jordan: Sounds good. We'll also capture benchmarks before/after and attach to the CRM deal.
00:11:26 Diego: I'm going to call out a config snippet I'll send: warmup_enabled=true; warmup_ramp_seconds=60; keepalive_rate_per_min=2; concurrency_soft_queue_ms=250; fallback_threshold_queue_pct=75.
00:11:45 Maya: That concurrency_soft_queue_ms number — what does it mean?
00:11:49 Diego: It's how long we allow requests to sit in a soft queue before spilling to fallback or returning a controlled error. It avoids instantly rejecting at the hard limit.
00:11:59 Evan: For our client library, what's the recommended header or tag for priority?
00:12:04 Diego: Use X-Redwood-Priority: high|normal|low, and X-Redwood-Route: checkout|autocomplete, etc. We'll include examples.
00:12:14 Leila: One more thing — could some of our 502s be coming from a downstream service call the model runtime does? Eg, a synchronous call to embeddings or an external cache?
00:12:25 Diego: Possible. We instrumented external call latencies and saw a small fraction of 502s correlated with an external logging service timeouts. We recommend setting an upstream deadline and circuit breaker for those calls.
00:12:38 Jordan: To summarize next steps: Diego sends probe scripts and config snippet; Evan runs probes and uploads traces; Jordan sends pilot warm-pool enablement steps and pricing update; Redwood will add telemetry metrics and an alert rule. Then reconvene on 2026-08-10 for results review.
00:12:58 Maya: Sounds good. Anything else?
00:13:02 Evan: Quick ask — can we get a short playbook doc for on-call: what to do in a 502 spike (check queue, check fallback_hits, toggle warm pool)?
00:13:12 Jordan: Yes we'll produce a 1-page playbook. Diego will draft it.
00:13:17 Leila: Great, thanks everyone.
00:13:20 Jordan: Thanks, we'll follow up in notes.
00:13:25 [call ends — remaining minutes used for quick config demo clipped from transcript]
notes: Included demo numbers from synthetic runs; customers asked for warm-pool toggle and probe scripts. Redwood to provide console metric patch and alert rule. Agreed follow-up benchmark on 2026-08-10.
